# Getting Started with RStudio {#sec-getting-started-with-rstudio}

::: {.guiding-question}
Guiding question: **How do I set up and navigate RStudio, the environment this module's instructions assume?**
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## By the end of this chapter you will be able to:
1. **Install** RStudio, after R itself.
2. **Navigate** its four panes: Console, Source, Environment/History and
   Files/Plots/Packages/Help.
3. **Create and run** an R script from inside RStudio.
4. **Find help** when something breaks.
:::

*(Source materials: Posit's official RStudio IDE user guide — see [Resources](resources.qmd).)*

## Who This Chapter Is For

If you've just installed R for the first time in [Rubric
9](09-getting-started-with-r.qmd), this chapter is the natural next step. RStudio is not
R itself — it's an **integrated development environment (IDE)**: a window around R that
adds a code editor, a file browser, a plot viewer and a few dozen conveniences, so you
rarely need R's own plain console. Every code example and screenshot elsewhere in this
module assumes you're working in RStudio (or [Positron](https://positron.posit.co/), its
newer sibling from the same company) rather than R's bare console.

::: {.callout-important}
Install R itself first (see [Rubric 9](09-getting-started-with-r.qmd)) — RStudio needs an
existing R installation to run and is useless without one.
:::

## Installing RStudio

Download **RStudio Desktop** (the free, open-source edition — that's all this module
needs) from [posit.co](https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/). Install it the same
way as any other application on your system. When you open it for the first time, RStudio
automatically detects the R installation from Rubric 9 and uses it in the background —
you won't normally interact with plain R directly again.

## Finding Your Way Around

RStudio's default layout splits into four panes, each with a specific job:

- **Source** (top-left): where you write and edit `.R` scripts or `.qmd` documents — the
  actual files you save and come back to.
- **Console** (bottom-left): where code actually runs and prints its output, one command
  at a time — the same console from Rubric 9, just inside this friendlier window.
- **Environment / History** (top-right): every variable you've created in this session,
  and what you've typed so far.
- **Files / Plots / Packages / Help** (bottom-right): a file browser, your rendered plots,
  installed packages and R's built-in help pages.

The official **[Posit RStudio IDE User Guide](https://docs.posit.co/ide/user/)** covers
this layout — and everything else about the IDE, from keyboard shortcuts to project
management — in much more depth than this short chapter can. Treat it as your reference
whenever something in RStudio's interface is unfamiliar.

::: {.exercise-box}
### Exercise 10.1 — Open RStudio and run a script

1. Open RStudio and locate the four panes described above.
2. In the **Source** pane, create a new R script (File → New File → R Script).
3. Type a short line, e.g. `print("Hello, RStudio")`, then run it with Ctrl+Enter
   (Windows/Linux) or Cmd+Enter (Mac) — the line should run in the Console below and
   print its output there.
4. Create a variable in the script (`y <- 5 * 5`) and run that line too. Find `y` listed
   in the Environment pane.

**Reflect:** which pane did the code's output appear in, and which pane shows the
variable you created? Being able to answer that quickly will save you time throughout
the rest of this module.
:::

::: {.differentiation-box}
::: {.struggling}
If the four-pane layout still feels overwhelming after Exercise 10.1: revisit the
[Posit RStudio IDE User Guide](https://docs.posit.co/ide/user/) and work through its
introductory tour slowly, pane by pane, with your own RStudio window open side by side —
it's written for exactly this situation.
:::
::: {.deeper}
Once the basics feel comfortable, the same guide covers RStudio Projects (keeping a
module's files self-contained — directly relevant to [Chapter
5](05-reproducible-research.qmd#organising-a-reproducible-project)) and keyboard shortcuts
that noticeably speed up day-to-day work.
:::
:::
